name: The Healthy Pipeline
source: Default definitions from the Solution Selling tradition. TO VALIDATE against B2B Klubben course material (see issue: Rubric v1 validation).

bands.label: not_addressed
bands.description: Dimension not meaningfully addressed, or no citable evidence exists.

bands.label: touched_unverified
bands.description: Raised in the meeting, but the evidence is seller-assumed; the customer did not confirm it in their own words.

bands.label: established
bands.description: Confirmed by the customer, directly and unambiguously.

bands.label: customer_articulated
bands.description: The customer articulated it unprompted or co-created it; strongest possible evidence.

dimensions.name: Pain
dimensions.definition: The customer has articulated a concrete, admitted business problem in their own words, with consequences.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for the customer describing a problem, its cost, or its consequences themselves. A seller stating the problem and the customer merely agreeing ('yes, exactly') is seller-assumed, not customer-stated. Note euphemistic or hedged Danish phrasing ('det er lidt en udfordring') as weaker evidence than concrete statements with numbers.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'We lose roughly two weeks per project on rework.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'So efficiency is the issue, right?' Customer: 'Mm.'

dimensions.name: Power
dimensions.definition: We know who owns the budget and the decision, and we are either talking to them or have a credible, agreed path to them.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for named roles and people, budget ownership, the decision process, and explicit requests for or grants of access to the economic buyer. A title alone is not power; confirmed decision authority is.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'The final call is mine, and I've set aside budget in Q1.'
dimensions.lowExample: No discussion of who decides or pays; seller assumes the contact person decides.

dimensions.name: Vision
dimensions.definition: The customer holds a concrete vision of solving the problem with our capabilities — ideally one they helped build.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for the customer describing a future state ('if we could X, then we would Y') connected to the seller's offering. Co-creation (customer extends or corrects the how) scores higher than passive acceptance of the seller's pitch.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'So if your model flags the risky projects each Monday, my team could reassign people the same week.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller describes the solution; customer listens without engaging with the how.

dimensions.name: Value
dimensions.definition: The value is quantified and agreed by the customer — the cost of the pain and the worth of solving it — not merely claimed by the seller.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look for numbers: hours, money, risk, opportunity — and for who states them. Customer-stated or customer-confirmed quantification scores high; seller-claimed ROI with no customer confirmation stays in the unverified band.
dimensions.highExample: Customer: 'If that saves each PM two hours a week, that is easily half a million kroner a year for us.'
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'This typically pays for itself in three months.' No customer response.

dimensions.name: Control
dimensions.definition: The seller controls the process: a clear, mutually agreed next step with owners, dates, and a path to decision.
dimensions.analysisGuidance: Look at how the meeting ends. A scheduled next meeting with an agreed purpose, named participants, and dates scores high. 'Send me some material and we'll be in touch' with no commitment scores low. A mutual action plan or agreed decision timeline is the strongest evidence.
dimensions.highExample: Agreed: workshop on the 14th with the CFO present; customer sends current process docs before then.
dimensions.lowExample: Seller: 'I'll send a proposal.' Customer: 'Great, thanks.' Nothing scheduled.
